hints: Look carefully at the words molecule versus fibre in options A and D. One collagen molecule is only the starting unit, a fibre is much bigger.
Recall the two famous facts about collagen: which tiny amino acid appears at every third position, and what type of strong cross-links join molecules into an insoluble fibre?
walkthrough:
**Remember what kind of protein collagen is**

Collagen is the classic fibrous protein. Think strength and support in skin, tendons and cartilage.

That means it is insoluble in water, very strong, and made of many polypeptides working together. That is quaternary structure.

**Sort out molecule versus fibre**

A single collagen molecule (tropocollagen) is three polypeptide chains wound together into a triple helix, held by hydrogen bonds.

A collagen fibre is much larger. It is many of these triple-helix molecules packed together and cross-linked.

**Check the special details**

Every third amino acid in each chain is glycine, because glycine is tiny enough to fit inside the tight helix. Not valine.

And the molecules are joined into fibres by strong covalent cross-links, not weak ionic bonds. This gives great tensile strength and insolubility.

So only option B describes collagen correctly.

options.A: This describes a single collagen molecule, not a fibre. A fibre contains many triple-helix molecules packed together.
options.B: Correct. Collagen is insoluble, fibrous for strength, and has quaternary structure because each molecule contains three polypeptides.
options.C: One-third of the residues are glycine, not valine. Glycine is needed at every third position to allow tight packing.
options.D: Molecules are linked into fibres by strong covalent cross-links, not ionic bonds, which gives collagen its strength and insolubility.
